div.p: We consider the problem of scheduling a set of preemptible independent periodic implicit-deadline hard realtime tasks on heterogeneous processors. We divide this problem into two sub-problems: (a) assigning portions of each processor (offline) to each task without jeopardizing schedulability; and (b) generating a schedule satisfying the assigned portions using an online semi-partitioned scheduler, called Heterogeneous Quasi-Partitioned Scheduling (hQPS). The scheduler handles task servers at run-time for ensuring that the processor shares assigned to tasks are timely available to them. Assessments indicate that the proposed solution (i) has good scalability (up to 64 tasks, 64 processors), (ii) is effective in generating schedules with few preemptions and few migrations, and (iii) is effective in managing resources; for task sets where an extra processor speed is required, our solution needs at most 10% extra compared to an optimal scheduler.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK
div.p: Heterogeneous multiprocessor architectures are increasingly used in modern computer systems. This has motivated the development of new solutions to the problem of scheduling a set of real-time tasks on a set of heterogeneous processors. Despite the advantages of having multiple types of processors, scheduling a set of tasks on this type of platform is harder compared to homogeneous processors. This is because the execution speed of a task at one time depends on the processor it executes on at that time [1].

A relevant result to the heterogeneous multiprocessor scheduling problem comes from Baruah [2], who optimally solved the feasibility problem for many-type heterogeneous processors via Linear Programming. This result can be taken as a theoretical baseline since practical aspects, such as job preemption or migration, were not taken into consideration. Other relevant results that consider more practical aspects are restricted to two-type heterogeneous multiprocessor [3]- [8], deal with uniform multiprocessors [9] or adopt partition-based scheduling algorithms [10]- [13]. More recently, Baruah et al. [14] addressed the problem of partitioning a set of sporadic tasks on heterogeneous multiprocessor platforms with an arbitrary number of types of processors. Again, their solution reduces the heterogeneous multiprocessor scheduling problem to a task partitioning problem as it does not allow migrations between different types of processors.

As modern heterogeneous architectures effectively support task migrations among different types of processors, a non-partitioned scheduling mechanism would be preferred [15]; also, it is known that partitioned scheduling cannot generate feasible optimal schedules. While task scheduling algorithms based on notions of fluid scheduling and fairness can be optimal (for both identical multiprocessor [16] and heterogeneous multiprocessor [2]), they may incur high scheduling overheads in the form of task preemptions and migrations.

Given the state-of-the-art in the heterogeneous multiprocessor scheduling problem, an important research question is the following: is it possible to schedule a set of realtime tasks on many-type processors with few preemptions and migrations without deviating excessively from Baruah's optimally result [2]?

Our contribution. We positively answer the posed research question for a set of preemptible independent implicit-deadline periodic hard real-time tasks. To the best of our knowledge, we describe the first scheduling algorithm for non-uniform heterogeneous processors that is not restricted to only twotype heterogeneous processors and present a solution for the scheduling problem with low preemption/migration overhead.

We solve the problem by addressing two sub-problems: (a) assigning portions of each processor to each task without jeopardizing schedulability, and (b) generating a schedule that satisfies the assigned task-to-processor portions. We approach sub-problem (a) by solving a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation in an offline fashion. Given the MILP solution, we derive a scheduling mechanism, also performed offline at the deployment stage, that explores the notion of task servers adapted from previous work [17], [18]. We derive an online scheduler to solve sub-problem (b). The derived scheduling scheme, called Heterogeneous Quasi-Partitioned Scheduling (hQPS), is mainly inspired by the QPS algorithm [18], [19]. Like the original QPS, hQPS distributes task portions into a set of servers. The servers are handled at run-time ensuring that the assigned processor shares are timely ensured to the tasks. This scheme works as a semi-partitioned scheduler, where some tasks might migrate during execution. From the viewpoint of servers, the hQPS scheme is similar to partitioned EDF, where local EDF on each local processor chooses which server to execute. Once scheduled, servers also use EDF as a client selection criteria.

Unlike the original QPS, which was not subject to processor-type constraints, hQPS has fewer choices to assign servers to processors and task portions to servers. Such con-straints in hQPS are captured by our new MILP formulation. Although not optimal in the sense that it cannot handle all feasible systems, extensive simulation shows that the distance from our MILP solution to the optimum was not greater than 10% and for all synthetically generated systems a feasible solution was found. For almost all generated systems, our scheme was capable of generating a valid schedule. The numbers of preemption and migration generated by hQPS were found to be very low compared to the state-of-art in heterogeneous processor scheduling.

Paper structure. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II introduces the model and notation used throughout the paper. Our main contribution is detailed in the task-to-processor assignment problem (Section III) and the hQPS algorithm (Section IV). To make the presentation more intuitive, we defer the MILP formulation to Section V to explain the reasons for the defined constraints. Experimental results are discussed in Section VI and final comments are given in Section VII.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL & NOTATION
div.p: We consider a set of n fully preemptive periodic tasks Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } to be scheduled on a system consisting of m heterogeneous processors. Any τ i ∈ Γ is defined by the tuple, τ i :(C i , T i ), with C i and T i representing respectively the worst-case execution time of τ i and its period. Any task τ i is released at instants kT i , k = 0, 1, . . . and any instance of τ i , called job J i,k , takes at most C i time units to execute on a processor of speed 1 and must finish by (k + 1)T i , its deadline. As the processors are heterogeneous, job execution time may differ depending on the processor it executes. We denote s i,p the speed of processor p as seen by the execution of τ i 's jobs. div.p: Any job of a task τ i may migrate from one processor to another during its execution. The remainder execution time of τ i at a given instant t, denoted e i,p,t , represents the time it takes from t to execute τ i 's current job on processor p. Note that if t is a job release time of τ i :(C i , T i ), e i,p,t = u i,p T i . Thus, if a job of τ i starts its execution on a processor p and executes there until time t when it migrates to processor p, its remainder execution on p can be computed as e i,p,t = e i,p ,t s i,p s i,p .
While jobs can be preempted or can migrate at any time during their execution, we make the usual assumption that there is no cost associated with preemption or migration.

div.head: III. TASK-TO-PROCESSOR ASSIGNMENT
div.p: The problem of scheduling the tasks in Γ on m heterogeneous processors can be divided into two sub-problems, task assignment and task scheduling. This section conveys the former.

A solution to the assignment problem is given by the association of portions of each task to a processor. Definition III.1 (Assignment matrix). Let Γ be a set of n tasks to be scheduled on m processors. Considering that the utilization of each task τ i ∈ Γ is defined according to (1) and (2), an assignment matrix X = {x i,p } n×m represents the fraction of processor p assigned to τ i as x i,p under the following constraints:

These constraints are the same used by [2] to specify necessary conditions for schedulability. Constraints (4)- (5) imply that the task portions assigned to a processor cannot exceed its capacity. These portions are specified as a value between 0 and 100%. Further, (6) means that the sum of all assigned portions of a task should cover 100% of its execution need. In our solution, determining the assignment matrix X is done offline via MILP, as will be detailed in Section V.

Example III.1 presents an assignment matrix for a system with four tasks and three processors. Constraints (4)-( 5) are clearly satisfied with all processors being fully utilized. Note that u i,p is not necessarily less than unity since some processors may not provide sufficient processing resources for some tasks. This is the case of τ 1 w.r.t. processor 2. HETEROGENEOUS QPS Heterogeneous QPS (hQPS) is an algorithm that builds on Quasi-Partitioning Scheduling (QPS) [18], an optimal solution for scheduling implicit-deadline tasks on homogeneous processors. This algorithm relies on the use of servers, which are execution proxies capable of ensuring that its clients (tasks or other servers) receive processing portions they need. These servers have been used in previous work [17], [18]. For making the paper self-contained its concept is described in Section IV-A.

Unlike the original QPS, which is free to assign tasks on the processors, hQPS is subject to an assignment matrix X. Hence, servers in hQPS must be defined following X and should avoid portions of the same task being scheduled in parallel on different processors. The mechanism ensuring this property, named master-slave servers, is presented in Section IV-B. In Section IV-C, the problem of allocating master-slave pairs is addressed. As will be seen, along with this allocation, the clients of the master servers are defined. Section IV-D describes an approach for assigning the remaining tasks to the other servers. Section IV-E presents the rules for dispatching the tasks and servers in the system. Section IV-F provides the proof of correctness.

div.head: A. Servers
div.p: Definition IV.1 (EDF server [17]). An EDF server σ, or simply server, can be defined by four attributes: its EDF scheduling policy; its set of clients, namely tasks or other servers assigned to σ, denoted cli(σ); its release time and deadline instants which include, but may not be limited to, all its clients' release times and deadlines; and a utilization, u σ , which represents the fraction of a processor demanded by σ, with 0 < u σ 1. Using similar notation for tasks, D(σ, t) represents the next deadline after t. At any instant r a server σ releases a job, its workload equals (D(σ, r)r)u σ . The jobs of server σ are subject to a scheduling algorithm but whenever σ is selected to execute, it schedules (via EDF) one of its clients to run.

Hereafter servers are referred to using symbol σ. We provide here an example that illustrates how servers work. To control the execution of task portions on any processor p, we also encapsulate each task portion into single-client servers with utilization equal to the corresponding portions. More than one of such single-client servers can then be encapsulated into other servers. See Example IV.1 for illustration.

Example IV.1. Consider an assignment matrix such that x 1,p = 0.4 and x 2,p = 0.2 for two tasks τ 1 and τ 2 , whose periods are 2 and 3, respectively. Single-client servers σ 1 and σ 2 with utilization u σi = x i,p are created, i = 1, 2. These two servers can then be scheduled by another server σ. Figure 1 shows a possible schedule.

Note that the workload released by each job of τ 1 and τ 2 on processor p is 0.4 × 2 = 0.8 and 0.2 × 3 = 0.6, respectively. That is, the behavior of σ 1 and σ 2 mimics that of their respective clients, namely the portions of τ 1 and τ 2 assigned to p. Now consider another server σ, assigned to processor p, which will be in charge of scheduling its clients σ 1 and σ 2 . Server σ must ensure that at least 60% of p is to execute its clients σ 1 and σ 2 . Since over-provisioning is not necessary, σ's utilization is defined as u σ = 0.6. From Definition IV.1, server σ releases a job at each instant one of its clients releases a job and the deadline of σ at any instant t equals the earliest deadline of its clients at t. For the illustrative example, D(σ, t) = min{D(σ 1 , t), D(σ 2 , t)}.

For notational convenience, for any processor p, we define the sets Γ p and S p that respectively contain all tasks and all servers assigned to processor p. That is, x i,p = 0 if and only if τ i ∈ Γ p . And σ ∈ S p implies that σ is a server allocated to p. As tasks can be assigned to more than one processor, the same task can belong to more than one set. Each server, on the other hand, is assigned only to one processor.

Figure 1 shows the behavior of a server σ allocated to a processor p. At time 0, σ releases a job with deadline 2. Its budget, defined at its release instant, represents its job workload. At time 0, this is equal to 0.6 × (2 -0) = 1.2. Once σ is scheduled on p, their client jobs are executed following EDF and its budget is consumed accordingly. At time 2, a new server job is released with workload equal to 0.6 × (3 -2) = 0.6, since the next deadline is at time 3. In the figure, τ represents a concurrent task/server running on p which sometimes has higher priority than σ, as can be seen at time 3.

Under the assumption that there is no other processor that executes τ 1 or τ 2 in parallel with their execution on p and that σ meets its own deadlines, the schedule generated by σ for τ 1 and τ 2 is valid on p, i.e., each job executes on at most one processor at each time instant and meets its deadline. This result comes from [17] and is restated below.

For generating a valid schedule one needs to ensure that no migrating task will ever have its portions scheduled in parallel at a given time by different servers. Next we present a solution for this problem in the form of extra constraints that must be in place for ensuring the correctness of the scheduling algorithm.

div.head: B. Managing migrating tasks via servers
div.p: In order to prevent that tasks assigned to more than one processor are scheduled to execute in parallel at run-time, hQPS defines a scheme based on a pair of servers for each migrating task, namely master and slave servers, both with the same utilization and sharing the same deadlines. While a master server is in charge of executing a migrating task, its slave server can execute any other task, except the migrating task the respective master executes. Master and slave servers are represented using superscript M and S, respectively; and a common subscript identifies the task they are dealing with. That is, σ M i and σ S i is a pair of master-slave servers defined for managing the execution of a migrating task τ i . The existence of a master server implies the existence of the corresponding slave and vice-versa. More formally,
div.formula: ∀i(∃σ M i ↔ ∃σ S i )(7)

div.p: The idea behind the master-slave scheme is making both servers in the same pair run in parallel but serving distinct clients. That is, whenever a master server executes on a processor, the execution of its corresponding slave is done on a different processor and each of them serves a disjunct set of tasks or other servers. Some masterslave allocation may produce hazard scenarios for scheduling and those also need to be ruled out. For example, as the execution of a master automatically enforces the execution of its slave, two masters that belong to distinct processors cannot have their corresponding slaves assigned to a common processor. The following constraint is to forbid this possibility.

div.p: Although this server allocation is as specified by the aforementioned constraints, it is not possible to ensure the parallelism of master-slave execution. If σ M i is selected to run on processor p, this enforces the execution of σ S i on p . However, no decision on processor p is possible since σ M k cannot execute as its slave is not able to run on p and σ S j cannot run either since its master on processor p was not selected. This kind of conflicting scenario can only occur when there is a cycle on a graph G X for a given assignment matrix X. We define a kind of assignment matrix X compatible with hQPS.

As a result, optimality is not ensured. Nevertheless, as will be seen, experimental results indicate that the proposed approach performs very well when compared to optimal solutions.
We next address the allocation of master-slave pairs for a given hQPS-compatible assignment matrix.

div.head: C. Defining and allocating master-slave pairs
div.p: Algorithm 1 describes a procedure that defines the necessary master-slave pairs according to a given assignment matrix. It also defines a rank for each processor. This ranking will be used during dispatching (Section IV-E) since scheduling decisions on processors with masters must occur before those with their slaves. The algorithm visits each connected component of the corresponding assignment graph. For each such component G X k , a breadth-first search (BFS) -the while loop -on its vertices (i.e., processors) is carried out.

The processor chosen at line 4 of Algorithm 1 defines the processor with the lowest rank in a connected component. This processor will be the root of a connected component and its choice, although does not affect the scheduling correctness, may influence the number of preemptions and migrations in the system. We use the heuristic of choosing the processor with the greater number of migrating tasks. This is done to obtain a greater number of subtrees under the chosen processor, aiming at subtrees with fewer processors and, consequently, lower interference caused by master-slave servers. A comparative study between this and other heuristics will be addressed in future work.

For each visited vertex p, each edge (p, p ) is then visited since it indicates the existence of at least a migrating task between p and p (the for loop at line 10). At lines 12-16, a pair of master-slave server is created per task that migrates between p and p with the master server allocated to p and its slave to p . That is, if there is more than one migrating task assigned to p, more than one master will be created and allocated to p. However, the same processor will never hold a master and its corresponding slave server. Neither will it contain slaves associated with distinct masters. This allocation strategy thus preserves the necessary constraints, as formally stated in Lemma IV.1.

Lemma IV.1. If X is an hQPS-compatible assignment matrix associated with a given system, Algorithm 1 allocates a master-slave pair per migrating task and the resulting allocation satisfies Constraints (7)-( 9) and (11). Moreover, any created master server provides the necessary bandwidth reservation for feasibly executing its client tasks.

Proof. According to Algorithm 1, each component of the assignment graph is dealt with at a time (lines 1 and 3). If there is no migrating task in the assignment X, there are as many components as tasks and no edges. This means that for each component G X k , a processor p is enqueued at line 7 and is dequeued at line 9. The loop of line 10 does not run since there is no edge (p, p ). As a result, no master-slave pair is created and the lemma follows.

Consider an assignment X with some migrating task and let G X k be a connected component of G X with more than one vertex. Consider p a vertex enqueued at line 7 or 19. As X is hQPS-compatible, Constraints ( 12)-( 13) tell that there is no path starting from p in G X k that returns to p after some edge (p, p ) is traversed. This means that p cannot be enqueued more than once. When p is dequeued, all edges from p are considered (line 10) and for each of these edges (p, p ), if any, a master-slave pair is created at lines 12-16, which is in accordance with Constraint (7). As p = p , Constraint (8) also holds. Furthermore, Constraint (9) follows since p = p and a single pair of master-slave servers is created per migrating task and allocated to p and p , respectively. Now suppose that two different master servers, σ M i ∈ S p and σ M i ∈ S p , are created at lines 12-16, with p = p . This means that their creation occurred when considering two distinct edges in G X in the loop of line 10. As the same edge is never traversed twice, due to line 17, and X is hQPS-compatible, the respective slave servers must have been allocated to distinct processors, which satisfies Constraint (11). Finally, for each migrating task τ i , its associated master allocated to processor p, has utilization set to x i,p , a value between 0 and 1, satisfying Definition IV.1. According to the assignment matrix X, x i,p is the processor share needed to execute τ i on p according to Constraints (4)-( 6).

Algorithm 1 iterates as in a classical BFS traversal. For each visited vertex, which represents a processor, the edges are traversed to enqueue its adjacent processors. Edges linking two processors are formed when there is at least a migrating task between them. As a result, the time complexity of the algorithm is O(n + m) for a system with n tasks and m processors since there cannot be more than n migrating task. Processors holding masters are ranked with a lower value than those processors with their respective slaves. During dispatching, this ranking will be observed along with EDF. The rules that define master-slave servers' deadlines will be given in Section IV-E, when dispatching is detailed.

Example IV.3. Taking the assignment matrix X for Example III.1, which is hQPS-compatible, and the corresponding assignment graph given in Example IV.2, Algorithm 1 allocates master-slave pairs as follows. Considering processor 1 as the first visited processor, masters σ M 1 , σ M 2 and σ M 3 are created and allocated to it. These servers are in charge of the portions of tasks τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 assigned to processor 1, respectively. Hence, their respective utilization values are set to 0.4, 0.4 and 0.2. The corresponding slaves, σ S 1 , σ S 2 and σ S 3 are defined. The former two slaves are allocated to processor 2 while the third is allocated to processor 3.

Algorithm 1 assigns a task to each master but does not define the slave's clients. Defining clients for masters is simpler since they are in charge of a single task portion. A slave may serve more than one task. We describe a procedure that assigns slave's clients next.

Example IV.4. Consider a processor p with two slaves, σ S 1 , σ S 2 and an independent server σ I with respective utilization values u σ S 1 = 0.3, u σ S 2 = 0.2 and u σ I = 0.5. Suppose they are jointly to server three tasks τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 for which the assignment matrix states that x 1,p = 0.5, x 2,p = 0.2 and x 3,p = 0.3. Further, due to Constraint (10), assume that σ S 1 cannot serve τ 1 and τ 2 cannot be a client of σ S 2 whereas τ 3 can be served by any of the three servers. A valid association could be cli(σ S 1 ) = {τ 2 , τ 3 }, cli(σ I ) = {τ 1 } and cli(σ S 2 ) = {τ 3 } with τ 3 being partially served by σ S 1 and σ S 2 . The edges from the source have capacities equal to the utilization of the corresponding clients. These have to be associated with slave or independent servers but this association is subject to the server utilization. The capacities for the edges linking server vertices to the sink considers this. Furthermore, when assigning tasks to slave servers, it is important to observe that the task in Γ p that is served by a master on another processor p cannot be associated with its slave on p. Note that the capacity function ω, as stated in Equation ( 14), removes this possibility, assigning 0 to the edge that links such a task to the slave whose master serves it on another processor.

div.p: MaxF is a classical LP formulation for the max-flow problem on the assignment flow network. The objective is to maximize the flow coming out from the source vertex o p . Constraint ( 16) is the flow conservation rule and ( 17) is to preserve the maximum capacity of the edges. Although there are polynomial-time solutions to the MaxF problem, in this work it is solved using the standard Ford-Fulkerson approach, which runs in pseudo-polynomial time O(f * |E p |) with f * representing the maximum flow value. The algorithm is available in classical textbooks [20].

Once the maximum flow through the edges is found, this can be translated into the client-to-server assignment as follows. The flow f (v, w), being it valid for a flow network N p , represents the capacity of server w that can be used to execute client v on processor p. If such a solution is optimal, no other client-to-server assignment is capable of increasing the service bandwidth for the tasks in Γ p . Lemma IV.2 associates the solution to the MaxF problem with the required client-toserver assignment.

At run-time, scheduling decisions necessary to execute the servers and their clients are made compatible with local EDF on each processor, as explained next.

div.head: E. Schedule generation
div.p: Once tasks and servers have been assigned to processors during an offline phase, the schedule is generated online by basically following local EDF in each processor and ensuring that master-slave pairs, if any, execute in parallel. Any processors with no slave servers are simply managed by local EDF. Master servers are scheduled likewise since there is no dependency on other servers. However, scheduling decisions for processors containing slave servers need to consider the master-slave pairs.

Let p and p be processors containing a master-slave pair, σ M and σ S , respectively. Algorithm 1 and the solution of the MaxF problem ensure that there is some task τ allocated to p and p such that τ , served by σ M , is not a client of σ S , as illustrated in Example IV.6. The parallel execution of both these servers, therefore, is valid as the execution of σ M on p forces the non-execution of τ on p . This scheme requires that (a) decisions on processor p are taken before those on p and (b) whenever σ S is forced to execute on p this causes no harms for the other servers assigned to p from the perspective of its local EDF scheduler. Requirement (a) is fulfilled by a dispatching that follows the processor ranking established by Algorithm 1, explained shortly. As for requirement (b), servers assigned to processors containing slave servers are configured to share their deadlines to make any execution order consistent with EDF. More specifically, master, slave and independent servers share all deadlines of tasks or servers assigned to the processor slave is assigned to, just as they were originally conceived by [18]. This is formalized as

div.p: Requirement (b), as expressed in (18), can be implemented in practice by keeping a deadline variable for each processor Algorithm 2: hQPS Dispatcher input: A set of processors P and their rank, the servers and their clients allocated to them (results of Algorithm 1 and MaxF problem). p containing slave servers, which should be equal to the minimum absolute deadline of the tasks assigned to p. Any server allocated to such processors will use this deadline when carrying out budget replenishment. At any time, any such server can be scheduled arbitrarily without violating EDF. Algorithm 2 gives a dispatching procedure that satisfies requirement (a). Each processor is visited following the ranking order defined by Algorithm 1 in its lines 6 and 18. This ensures that processors with masters are visited before those containing their respective slaves. For each visited processor p, if there is no slave on it, local EDF is applied (lines 5 and 7). Otherwise, the slave running on p is selected when its masters were previously selected to execute (line 10). If this is not the case, an independent server is selected instead (line 12). The loop of line 13 is to schedule the tasks in those selected servers. Dispatching servers according to this scheme ensures that no server misses its deadlines, as will be shown.

hQPS selects the tasks to be dispatched similarly to QPS. The procedure is executed whenever a task or server has a job arrival or job complete event. Recall from Algorithm 1 that there are processor ranks. Algorithm 2 takes these ranks into account. It visits processors starting from rank 1 and follows a non-descending order of ranks (lines 1,3-4). As a result, masters are selected before their respective slaves, ensuring their parallel execution.

div.head: F. Correctness of Heterogeneous QPS
div.p: Hereafter we refer to the hQPS scheduling scheme as a set of servers and their clients, defined according to Algorithm 1 and by solving the MaxF problem, as stated in Definitions IV.5 and IV.6, with independent servers in line with Definition IV.4 and with all servers and tasks dispatched according to Algorithm 2. Next, we show the correctness of hQPS.
We first observe that the hQPS scheduling scheme preserves the schedulability of servers.

Lemma IV.3. Consider an hQPS-compatible assignment matrix X for a system composed of a set of heterogeneous processors. Under the hQPS scheme, no server misses any of its deadlines as long as Constraint (18) holds.
Proof. We first observe that since X is a hQPS-compatible matrix, the following constraints hold: (4)-( 6) (by definition), ( 7)-( 9), and (11) (by Lemma IV.1) and ( 12)-( 13) (by definition).

If there is no migrating task, no server will be assigned to any processor by Algorithm 1. In this case, there is nothing to prove. Consider the case where servers are allocated to some processors. As Constraint (13) holds, Algorithm 1 cannot visit the same processor more than once. Thus, its line 6 and the processor visit order in the loop of line 8 ensure that there is at least a processor p containing a master with rank 1 and p has no slave servers. For each such a processor p, Algorithm 2 follows local EDF, which means that the lemma holds for p as EDF is optimum and Constraints (4)- (6) imply that no processor is overloaded. Now let p be a processor with some master server σ M whose slave is assigned to another processor p . We first claim that any server that is not a client of another server meets its deadlines. Constraint (18), which holds by assumption, tells us that σ M , σ S and any other server running on p share the same deadlines. Further, we know from Constraint (11) that two masters that belong to distinct processors cannot have their corresponding slaves assigned to the same processor. Therefore, whenever σ M is selected to run on p, forcing the execution of σ S on p , the generated schedule on p is conforming to local EDF. As a result, any server assigned to p , slave or independent, will meet all their deadlines due to EDF optimality, which shows the claim. In order to see that the lemma holds for any server, we observe that a server cannot be a client of more than one server. This is due to the MaxF problem. Recall that Definition IV.5 defines clients for slave or independent servers as tasks or master servers and masters' clients can only be tasks, whose assignment is by Algorithm 1. Hence, the masters that are clients of other servers also meet their deadlines, which follows from Theorem IV.1 since their servers meet theirs. Therefore, all servers meet their deadlines.
Under the conditions stated in Lemma IV.3, no task misses any of its deadlines, as shown in Theorem IV.2.

Theorem IV.2. Let Γ be a set of periodic tasks, feasible on a set of heterogeneous processors, and consider an hQPScompatible assignment matrix X for this system. The hQPS scheme applied to Γ under X ensures that no task misses any of its deadlines as long as Constraint (18) holds true.

Proof. For those tasks not scheduled by servers, if any, we know by the hQPS scheme (Algorithm 2, lines 7 and 17) that they are scheduled according to local EDF. The theorem holds for this case by the optimality of EDF and by the fact that Constraints (4)-( 6) are valid for X.

Let us now focus on the schedulability of tasks that are clients of some server. Without loss of generality, let τ i be one of these tasks. There are two cases to be considered depending on whether τ i is a client of a single or more than one server. In the former case, since we know from Lemma IV.3 that τ i ' server meets any of its deadlines, Theorem IV.1 informs us that τ i also meets its deadlines. For the latter case, let x i,p and x i,p respectively be the portions of τ i assigned to processors p and p . Recall from Constraint (12) that τ i cannot be assigned to more than two processors. As τ i is a migrating task, there must be a master server σ M i in charge of τ i in some processor, say p. From the hQPS scheme (Algorithm 2), whenever σ M i runs on p, its slave σ S i also executes on p . As the MaxF solution does not admit τ i as a client of σ S i , τ i cannot be served on p at the same time as it is served on p. Therefore, for the sake of analysis, we can think of τ i as being two independent tasks, τ p i and τ p i , with execution times respectively equal to x i,p and x i,p , both with the same period as τ i and to be scheduled on p and p , respectively. Again, as τ p i and τ p i are clients of servers that meet all their deadlines, from Theorem IV.1 we know that they also meet theirs, implying that τ i is correctly scheduled.

div.head: V. MILP FORMULATION
div.p: As we discussed in Section IV, obtaining an assignment solution X requires that the graph obtained from X is a tree (i.e., does not have a cycle). Therefore, in this section, we explain how to state that X must satisfy the constraint that the assignment solution has no cycle.

Recall that n and m denote the number of tasks and processors, respectively. We let {a..b} denote the set of integers a and b. We let < a, b > denote a tuple with two elements a and b. We will let i be an integer in {1..n}; intuitively, this is a task index. We will let p be an integer in {1..m}; intuitively, this is a processor index. Ditto for p and p .

If it holds for an assignment solution X that the above constraints are satisfied, then the graph corresponding to X is a tree (i.e., does not have a cycle). div.head: VI. ASSESSMENT
div.p: We experimentally evaluate the distance of hQPS from an optimal solution using our MILP formulation for systems considered feasible by Baruah's LP-formulation. We also provide numbers for the execution time required to solve the MILP. Further, results regarding the online behavior of hQPS using the average number of preemption and migration per job during execution are also reported. Some constraints we introduced in our scheduling scheme may rule out some assignment matrices X for which there is a schedule according to which no tasks miss their deadlines. Constraint (8), for example, is imposed by the master-slave scheme, so that no task is assigned to more than two processors. As a consequence, hQPS is not expected to deliver an optimal scheduling solution.

Section V presented our MILP formulation which gives an offline assignment for tasks to processors while eliminating undesired cycles. Using the Gurobi solver, we have implemented a software tool that takes a system (taskset with ratedescription and number of processors) as input and outputs a valid assignment matrix X. Experiments were carried out in the following settings. Systems were generated with a number of tasks, ntasks ∈ {1, 4, 16, 64}, and a number of processors, nprocessors ∈ {1, 4, 16, 64}. Each generated system is characterized by three parameters: T maxexponent, We then set T i to 2 raised to the power of that number. Also, for each task τ i , we generated a uniformly distributed number in [1, utilminexponent]. We then set utilization of task τ i to 2 raised to the power of minus that number. Then we compute C i as utilization of τ i multiplied by T i . Finally, for each task τ i , for each processor p, we generated a uniformly distributed number in [1, rminexponent]. Then we compute u i,p as 2 raised to the power of minus that number. Thus, tasksets have high diversity.

After optimally solving our MILP formulation the objective function value indicates how loaded the system is. Similar to Baruah's LP-formulation [2], an objective function not greater than 1.0 means that the system is feasible under all constraints. An objective function greater than 1.0 reflects the worsening caused by this approach. For all feasible systems, we also ran the scheduler simulation to evaluate the results in terms of preemption and migration overhead.

Table I presents the found results. The time required (in seconds) to solve a MILP problem was obtained for an Intel i7 Skylake processor with 32 GB of memory. The value obtained for the objective function (OF) is also presented in the same table. For each cell named Time and OF, we report the maximum number observed for all experiments for that cell. All synthetically generated systems were verified to be feasible according to Baruah's LP-formulation [2]. Only those considered feasible were then verified against hQPS. Therefore, the results in the table express the observed worstcase distance to an optimal solution. The maximum values for the objective function l are reasonably close to 1 under hQPS, being equal to 1 in most cases. The running time taken by the solver also seems reasonable. The worst observed value was about three hours, which is admissible for a procedure performed offline.

As for average preemption (P) and migration (M) per job, the systems were simulated for 100 times the maximum period in the task set. As can be seen, on average, the observed number of preemption or migrations are relatively low. This confirms the effectiveness of the hQPS scheme.

We also compared hQPS against Hetero-Wrap [6], which is optimal for two-type heterogeneous systems. For this com-parison, we used the same specification as the one described by the authors. A total of 10, 000 feasible task systems were generated for each interval of total utilization. Eight such intervals were considered, (0.2, 0.3], (0.3, 0.4], . . . , (0.9, 1.0]. The total utilization of a task set is computed as i (u 1 i + u 2 i )/(m 1 + m 2 ), as suggested by Chwa et al [6], where u j i is the execution rate required by task i on processor of type j and m j the number of processors of type j. The feasibility of each system was verified according Baruah's LPformulation [2].

The number of processors m j {2, 3, 4} of each type j ∈ {1, 2} and the number of tasks in the range [m 1 + m 2 , 25] were chosen according to a Uniform distribution. Further, the utilization for each type of processor was randomly chosen in the range [0.1, 2.0]. The manner task periods were set was not given by Chwa et al. In our experiments, task periods were uniformly distributed within [1,100].

Regarding schedulability, only 0.38% of the generated task sets with total utilization within (0.9, 1.0] could not be handled. For all other intervals, 100% of the task sets were feasibly scheduled by hQPS. The highest value found for the objective function (OF) was 1.0231, indicating that even this set of tasks would be successfully scheduled by hQPS if processors were only 2.31% faster.

For all systems considered feasible by hQPS (a total of 79, 962 systems out of 80, 000), we checked the number of preemptions and migrations against Hetero-Wrap. Table II shows the results. As expected, hQPS performs much better since it inherits the characteristics of QPS (a nor-fair algorithm) while Hetero-Wrap (based on fairness) is bound to generate more preemption and migration points.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: We present a new solution to the multiprocessor scheduling problem of preemptible independent periodic real-time tasks on heterogeneous platforms with several types of processors. We design and implement the Heterogeneous Quasi-Partitioned Scheduling (hQPS) that works as a semipartitioned scheduler by satisfying the assigned task-toprocessor portions given by our proposed MILP formulation, while allowing only some specific tasks to migrate during execution. Because of this strategy, hQPS produces task schedules with relatively low number of migrations and preemptions per job. We show that our MILP formulation can provide optimal solutions for most cases and close (10%) to the optimum in other cases.
